title: Joys and hopes (Gaudium et Spes 1)
hook: nothing genuinely human fails to echo in the hearts of Christ's followers
tomorrow: when every feed has an opinion, whose voice is left?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two instincts about Mary and one guardrail: her motherhood in grace continues, and she takes nothing from him.

The kitchen TV is on low. A flood somewhere far away: brown water up to the porch roofs, a man wading with a dog in his arms. Then an ad for car insurance. Then the weather. The sound of other people's disasters is part of the background hum of a weeknight, and it passes in seconds. Vatican II's document on the Church in the modern world opens its very first sentence on that hum, and refuses to let it pass.
screen: `A FLOOD ON THE KITCHEN TV.` → `THEN AN AD. THEN THE WEATHER.` → `IT PASSES IN SECONDS.`

segments.voice: The document is named for its first words, Gaudium et Spes: joy and hope. The sentence comes in four parts. First, the list: the joys and the hopes, the griefs and the anxieties of people today. It doesn't stop at the happy half. Second, who comes first: especially, the council says, those who are poor or in any way afflicted. Third, the turn. These, it says, are the joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of the followers of Christ as well. Not watched from a distance. Theirs. Then the line the day hangs on: nothing genuinely human fails to raise an echo in their hearts. Fourth, the reason. The Church, the paragraph says, is made of human beings, so it knows itself bound to the whole human race and its history. Paul had put the instinct in one line to the Romans: "Rejoice with them that rejoice; weep with them that weep." And the next paragraph of the council's document widens the address on purpose. It speaks not only to Catholics, but to all people. The man wading with his dog belongs in that first sentence.
screen: `JOYS, HOPES, GRIEFS, ANXIETIES.` · `THE POOR AND AFFLICTED FIRST.` · `THEIRS ARE OURS.` · `ADDRESSED TO ALL PEOPLE.` · then, large: `NOTHING HUMAN IS FOREIGN.`

segments.voice: Let your ears go out past the room: traffic, a neighbor's TV, a bird, a pipe knocking. Choose one sound another person made, and stay with it, knowing there's a whole day behind it, a joy or a worry you'll never hear about. If you pray, hold that unknown person in the quiet.
Joys and hopes. The council's first words to the modern world: everyone's joys and griefs, taken as its own.
Your line: nothing human is foreign. The flood far away is close enough to echo. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1586 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHEN EVERY FEED HAS AN OPINION, WHOSE VOICE IS LEFT?`

howItsDone: Catholics often quote the opening of Gaudium et Spes when speaking of the Church's care for the poor and suffering, and parishes bring the world's needs into the prayers of the faithful at Mass.

fork.setup: your group chat goes from a friend's engagement photos to a fundraiser for a stranger whose house burned. someone types "not our problem, we don't know her." what would Gaudium et Spes 1 say?
options: only the engagement belongs; a stranger's fire isn't ours.
both belong: joys and griefs alike echo in Christ's followers.
only the fire belongs; celebrating is a distraction now.
fork.reveal: the first sentence holds joys and hopes, griefs and anxieties together, the afflicted named first, and says nothing genuinely human fails to echo in Christ's followers.

chat.says: Lupe saw a flood on the news and cried at dinner. tía says just turn it off. should i?
options: Turn it down, not her heart off. Pray for those families together; their grief can be yours too.
Yes, totally. Other people's disasters aren't really her business, and it'll only upset her.
No, leave it on. Kids need to see all of it so they toughen up about the world early.
chat.meaning: Gaudium et Spes 1: the griefs and anxieties of people, especially the afflicted, belong to Christ's followers too. Nothing genuinely human leaves them untouched.

Gaudium et Spes.meaning: Vatican II's document on the Church in the modern world

Vatican II.meaning: the Second Vatican Council, a gathering of the world's Catholic bishops

afflicted.meaning: suffering, in body, mind or circumstance

Romans.meaning: Paul's letter to the Christians in Rome, in the New Testament

sources.work: Second Vatican Council, Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World

sources.quoted: Rejoice with them that rejoice; weep with them that weep.

notes: Gaudium et Spes 1–2 paraphrased (official English not public domain): confirm 'the joys and the hopes, the griefs and the anxieties of the men of this age, especially those who are poor or in any way afflicted', 'nothing genuinely human fails to raise an echo in their hearts', the community 'composed of men', 'linked with mankind and its history by the deepest of bonds', and GS 2's address to the whole of humanity.
The carry 'nothing human is foreign' echoes Terence's well-known line, not the council's wording. The Keeper may prefer a carry closer to GS 1.
Romans 12:15 quoted from Douay-Rheims; confirm exact wording. Paul's line is offered as the script's link, not as a citation the council makes in GS 1.
